policies.scope: Some software-engineering interview loops; confirm your invitation
policies.body: Reporting describes AI-assisted code comprehension and evaluation of AI fluency. The format is a pilot; the reports do not establish a universal round count, codebase length, editor, or permission to use any assistant in every interview.
Responsible AI use is encouraged for preparation. Assessments and interviews require independent demonstration of skills unless outside assistance is explicitly permitted.

policies.scope: Published hiring process; role-specific details still vary
policies.body: The hiring page says an in-person onsite is part of the process before an offer and prohibits unapproved outside tools such as ChatGPT during interviews. Confirm the setup with your recruiter.

Canva describes interactive AI-skills challenges for engineering. The recruitment partner explains the expected setup. This is an example of why another employer’s rules cannot be assumed to apply to Google or Microsoft.

policies.scope: DeepMind roles; distinct from Google SWE hiring
policies.body: Its interview guide permits AI for preparation but asks candidates not to use AI during live interviews or tasks unless told otherwise. Its process is managed separately from Google recruiting.
policies.source: Google DeepMind candidate guide; reviewed 29 October 2026

recruiterQuestions: Which interview rounds apply to my role, location, and level?
Will there be an existing-code comprehension, debugging, or AI-assisted exercise?
Which tools are allowed in each round, and is an assistant provided?
What language, editor, test runner, and collaboration setup will I use?
How should I request accommodations or report a tool failure?

drills.title: Repair a binary-search boundary
drills.brief: Read the function without running it. Find a case where the target exists but is never checked. State the loop invariant, make the smallest repair, and test it.
drills.review: The active interval is inclusive, so the final candidate still needs examination. Use while (left <= right). The empty interval starts with right=-1, so no element is accessed. Prove why each update discards only impossible candidates.
drills.aiTask: If your mock explicitly allows an assistant, ask for a counterexample before asking for a patch. Reject a patch that reads nums[0] on an empty input.

drills.title: Review an apparently correct prefix-sum patch
drills.brief: A teammate replaced long long with int to reduce memory use. Find a failing input and explain why passing the small examples does not validate the change.
drills.review: Individual int values can be valid while their accumulated sum exceeds int range. Signed overflow is undefined behavior in C++. Keep the prefix storage and returned result in long long; ensure arithmetic is widened before an addition that could overflow. Clarify query bounds separately.
drills.aiTask: Ask an allowed assistant to justify the numeric range. Verify the bound independently, rather than accepting “the compiler will handle it.”

drills.title: Define the instant a cache entry expires
drills.brief: The TTL contract says an entry is expired at now >= expires. Inspect this implementation and give a deterministic boundary test.
drills.review: The comparison must be >=. Injecting a clock or passing now makes the test reproducible. Then handle a missing key explicitly with get(), and consider which clock is appropriate. This exercise is about the boundary contract, not a production-ready concurrent cache.
drills.aiTask: If assistance is permitted, request tests around the equality boundary and a missing key. Explain each test yourself.
